analytic.title: Utilization Bounds for RM Scheduling on Uniform Multiprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Utilization bounds for Earliest Deadline First(EDF) and Rate Monotonic(RM) scheduling are known and well understood for uniprocessor systems. In this paper, we derive limits on similar bounds for the multiprocessor case, when the individual processors need not be identical. Tasks are partitioned among the processors and RM scheduling is assumed to be the policy used in individual processors. A minimum limit on the bounds for a 'greedy' class of algorithms is given and proved, since the actual value of the bound depends on the algorithm that allocates the tasks. We also derive the utilization bound of an algorithm which allocates tasks in decreasing order of utilization factors. Knowledge of such bounds allows us to carry out very fast schedulability tests although we are constrained by the fact that the tests are sufficient but not necessary to ensure schedulability.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time systems are characterised by explicit timing constraints. Tasks in such systems typically have known execution times (probabilistic or deterministic) and a deadline before which they must be completed. Traditionally, systems which handled these tasks had a single processor and thus, much work has been done in the modeling and analysis in the context of uniprocessor systems. But, as multiprocessor systems become ubiquitous, the need for fast and efficient scheduling algorithms for such systems is on the rise. It is well known that the results derived in the uniprocessor case do not necessarily carry over directly to the multiprocessor case [6]. Multiprocessor systems can be classified into 3 broad categories [1]: Identical: In such systems, all the processors that constitute the multiprocessor are identical in all aspects. Any given task takes the same amount of time to run on any of the processors. Uniform: In such sytems, the processors are not identical, but each processor is characterised by a 'capacity'. The time that any given task takes to complete execution on that processor, is inversely proportional to the 'capacity' of that processor. Capacity can be thought of as the speed of that processor. Heterogeneous: Here, the system is characterised by a rate matrix, which associates a rate of execution with each processor-task pair. The time that a given task takes to run on a processor depends on how well the task is matched to that processor. In this paper, we will exclusively deal with the uniform multiprocessing model. As Funk et al [5] point out, the model of the uniform multiprocessor is of great relevance in application systems. System designers may want the freedom to use non-identical processors in their multiprocessor systems. Also, with multi-core processors becoming commonplace, cores with different processing capacities to handle dynamic workloads may not be far away. Sometimes, some fraction of computing capacities of processors in identical multiprocessor systems may be dedicated to some tasks, forcing us to model such a system as one with processors of varying capacities. Thus, such a system model is useful and relevant. A schedule is an assignment of the given computational tasks to available processors. There are 2 broad approaches to scheduling in Multiprocessor Systems-the global, and the partitioned approach. Global: In the global approach, tasks are allowed to migrate to another processor after having completed part of their execution on some processor. In such systems, care should be taken to transfer the context information to the processor where the task will be subsequently run. Partitioned: In contrast to the above, there is the partitioned approach, in which if a task starts execution on one processor, it is constrained to run only on that processor. Well known uniprocessor algorithms can then be used on the individual processors. In this paper, we deal exclusively with the partitioned approach. The Rate Monotonic(RM) algorithm is a well studied fixed priority algorithm in the context of uniprocessor systems. Fixed priority algorithms assign the same priority to all jobs of a given task. The utilization bound offered by the RM algorithm(in the uniprocessor case) is m(2 1/m -1), where m is the number of tasks in the system. Once the scheduling algorithm on the individual processors has been fixed, the problem of multiprocessor scheduling boils down to one of partitioning the given task set among the processors that constitute the system. There is a class of allocation algorithms which we call the 'greedy' or 'reasonable' class of algorithms. This refers to those algorithms in which no task is refused execution if some processor can accomodate that task. Examples of such algorithms are First fit, Best fit, Worst fit etc. This research: We have derived the minimum limit on the utilization bounds of a task set for the case when a greedy algorithm is used to partition the tasks among the processors and the RM algorithm is used on the individual processors. This means that the utilization bound given by any algorithm belonging to the greedy class will be equal to, or above the minimum limit. We have also derived the utilization bound of the algorithm that performs allocations according to decreasing order of task utilization factors.

Previous Work: Our work builds on the work of Lopez et al [7] who derived similar limits for the utilization bounds in the identical multiprocessor case. We generalize the results to the case when the processors are not identical. Baruah et al [3] look at similar bounds when interprocessor migration among tasks is allowed, that is, under the global scheduling paradigm.

Organization of this report: Section 2 describes the system model in detail. In section 3, we provide and prove the minimum limit on the utilization bound of a task set for the greedy/reasonable class of algorithms. Section 4 describes a particular algorithm that arranges the tasks in decreasing order of utilization and derives its utilization bound. In section 5, we discuss the results and give an example. Concluding remarks and some future directions are provided in section 6.

div.head: System Model and Definitions
div.p: The various components of the model are enumerated below:

• Processors: Let there be n not necessarily identical processors in the system. Let us denote the set of processors by Π={π 1 , π 2 ...π n }. Without loss of generality, we arrange the processors in order of increasing speed. The capacity k j of a processor j where 1 ≤ j ≤ n is defined as the ratio of the speed of π j to the speed of π 1 . Thus, k j ≥ 1.0 ∀j = 1, 2...n. Also, by definition, k 1 =1.0. The capacity of this uniform multiprocessor system is defined as κ = n j=1 k j .

• Tasks: Let τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ....τ m } be a set of tasks with computation times {C 1 , C 2 , .....C m },(measured on the processor with capacity 1.0) and periods {T 1 , T 2 , ....T m }. Let us assume that the tasks have deadlines equal to the periods. The tasks are assumed to be pre-emptible. Utilization of task
div.formula: τ i (1 ≤ i ≤ m) is defined as u i = C i /T i .
div.p: The utilizations are assumed to be bounded from above by a parameter α, 0 < u i ≤ α, where α is measured on the processor π 1 . Hereafter, all utilizations are wrt the processor π 1 , unless otherwise mentioned explicitly.
The cumulative utilization (or just Utilization) of the task set τ is defined as
div.formula: U τ = m j=1 u i .
div.p: • Within a processor, it is assumed that the Rate Monotonic(RM) scheduling algorithm is used.

• The allocation algorithm used is assumed to belong to the 'greedy' or 'reasonable' [8] class, defined as: A greedy algorithm is one which fails to allocate a ready task to a processor, if and only if there is no processor which can hold the task.

A feasible schedule is defined as one in which a task is assigned to at most one processor, and every task completes by its deadline. Otherwise, the task set is said to be infeasible on the given system. An algorithm is said to have a utilization bound U if it can guarantee that any task set τ with a utilization U τ ≤ U can be feasibly scheduled on the system in question.

div.head: Proof
div.p: We will show that if a set of tasks τ cannot be feasibly scheduled by a greedy algorithm, the utilization of that task set U τ necessarily exceeds U RM-Greedy NI-lower .

div.head: An example
div.p: Consider a uniform multiprocessor system with 4 processors of capacities 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5. This may correspond to a set of processors of speeds, say, 100MHz, 150MHz, 200MHz, and 250 MHz. Let the number of tasks in the system be given to be 50. div.head: Conclusions and future work
div.p: In this paper, we stated and proved the minimum limit on the utilization bound guarantees that the 'greedy' class of algorithms can provide. Such bounds can enable us to carry out fast tests to determine if a given set of real time tasks are feasibly schedulable on the given uniform multiprocessor platform. We do not put any restriction on how the processors are arranged before making allocations. We derived the utilization bound for the GAD algorithm. We investigated how the bound varies as the parameter α is varied. There may exist some algorithm which has a utilization greater than the GAD algorithm too. Similar bounds in the heterogeneous multiprocessor model when the system is described by a rate matrix are yet to be explored.
